title: Where it grows
subtitle: Loire, Bordeaux and the New World

steps.title: France
steps.body: Cabernet Franc's two French homes are the Loire, where it makes single-variety reds, and Bordeaux, where it's a blending grape, especially on the Right Bank. It also grows in the south-west. In the Loire it's sometimes called Breton; in Saint-Émilion, Bouchet.

steps.title: Cool and warm
steps.body: Cabernet Franc tolerates cold winters better than Cabernet Sauvignon, and ripens earlier. That suits the Loire, northern Italy and even Canada and New York. In warmer places, like Argentina's Valle de Uco, California, Virginia and Hungary's Villány, it gives riper, fuller wines, with fewer green notes.

steps.prompt: Match each region to its Cabernet Franc.
steps.explanation: Cabernet Franc is gaining attention well beyond France.

steps.body: Argentina's Cabernet Franc from the Valle de Uco has become one of the country's most exciting new wines, rivalling Malbec for critics' attention.

steps.prompt: Why does Cabernet Franc suit cooler regions?
options: It ripens earlier than Cabernet Sauvignon
steps.explanation: It doesn't need extreme heat, and it buds earlier, not later.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Cabernet Franc is single-variety in the Loire and blended in Bordeaux
It's cold-hardy and ripens earlier than Cabernet Sauvignon
Argentina, California, Virginia and Hungary grow fine examples
